items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.

items.title: Porter's framework asks about industry structure, not firms
items.claim: Michael Porter's 1979 HBR article introduced the five forces framework. What does it analyse?

options.text: The structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes

items.reveal:
Porter's 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' (HBR, March 1979) made a structural argument: average industry profitability is set by the strength of the five forces. Some industries (pharma, software platforms) are persistently profitable; others (airlines, supermarkets) persistently low-margin.

McGahan and Porter (1997) found industry effects explained 19% of business unit profitability variance — less than firm effects (32%) but real. Critics (including Henry Mintzberg) argue the framework underweights innovation, complementors and network effects, which 1979 industry economics didn't see clearly.
items.why: Strategy starts with which industry you're competing in, not how cleverly you compete. Some industries make it nearly impossible to earn supernormal returns.

items.title: Market research said the Walkman would fail
items.claim: Sony launched the TPS-L2 Walkman in 1979. What did market research suggest beforehand?

options.text: Strong demand from young consumers — supporting the launch
Likely failure: consumers reported they wanted recording capability, not just playback, and disliked the absence of speakers
No research was conducted because Akio Morita had no money for it

items.reveal:
Co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted a portable player so he could listen to opera on long flights. Akio Morita, despite hostile focus group findings, championed the launch. Sony hedged by initially offering it with two headphone jacks (so you could share) and a 'hotline' button to talk to a companion — both later dropped.

First-month sales in Japan were 30,000 units. By the early 1980s the Walkman was a global phenomenon and 'walkman' became a generic word for portable cassette player.

Clayton Christensen later used the case in 'The Innovator's Dilemma' to argue that existing customer research can't reliably predict demand for genuinely new products.
items.why: Market research has methodological limits. Consumers can tell you what they want among options they already know; they're worse at imagining a category that doesn't exist.
